summary:
Same-sex conduct has not been criminalised in Haiti since 1791. The legal framework provides no recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not function as a protection avenue in practice, so a trans visitor has no statutory remedy to invoke and no aggravated-penalty framework behind any complaint.

Two Senate measures would tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. As of November 2017 both awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies; the sources in this inventory do not record a later status for either bill.

The certificate itself is a live obstacle for people whose orientation or identity becomes visible: it is required by many employers and schools, and homosexuality is listed among the offences that can justify refusing it. The June 2017 bill would regulate who receives the certificate, which directly affects students and young job seekers.

The United States State Department's 2018 report on Haiti recorded that attitudes "remained hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince". For a visibly trans visitor this is a direct climate warning, not a legal one: the exposure arises from visibility itself rather than from any offence.

Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, Haiti's national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019. The Washington Blade reported that poisoning was alleged but unconfirmed, and ILGALAC issued a mourning statement. This is the most recent documented death of a trans- or LGBT-linked figure in this record; no later instance is documented here.

Human Rights Watch's 2018 world report states that LGBT persons in Haiti continued to face high levels of discrimination. The documented pattern is concealment rather than legal sanction: LGBTQ people often hide their orientation or gender identity for fear of discrimination, and trans people face documented harassment in displacement camps established after the 2010 earthquake.
tangentialFactors:
The distance between formal rights and lived exposure is the central context. The 1987 Constitution guarantees all citizens a right to health care, housing, education, food and social security, yet people who disclose an LGBTQ identity are routinely refused those services in practice, so the guarantees give a visitor little practical cover.

The hostility documented in the 2018 US State Department report is concentrated in the capital, Port-au-Prince, where a visibly trans visitor would be most exposed and where the 2019 death of a national advocacy leader occurred. The record contains no comparable documentation for other cities, which reflects the sourcing rather than a demonstrated difference.

Post-disaster conditions are the documented setting for trans-specific harassment: camps established after the 2010 earthquake are where harassment of transgender people is recorded. Following the same disaster, gay and bisexual men reported adopting a more masculine demeanour to avoid harassment and to reduce the risk of being denied emergency housing, health care and food-for-work programmes — an indicator of how quickly services are withheld from people read as LGBTQ.
localsOnly:
The Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs is a resident-facing gatekeeping instrument: many employers and schools require it, and it lists homosexuality as an offence capable of justifying refusal. For Haitian students and job seekers, the June 2017 Senate bill on regulating the certificate is therefore an employment and education question, not merely a symbolic one.

Constitutional entitlements to education, health care, housing, food and social security exist on paper for citizens, but LGBTQ Haitians report concealing their identity to reach them. The 1987 Constitution guarantees the right to education while LGBTQ youth face pervasive social hostility in schools.

HIV figures in this record are dated: prevalence rose to 4–6% as of 2008 overall and 13% in certain rural neighbourhoods in the same period. Grasadis, founded in 1997, works on HIV/AIDS prevention among the LGBTQ population. These figures describe 2008 and should not be read as current prevalence.

Kouraj operates as the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, and ILGALAC, the regional body, tracks and responds to killings; both are the visible institutional targets in a hostile climate, as the November 2019 death of Kouraj's president indicates.
outOfScopeNotes:
Prison placement for trans detainees is unresolved in this record. No rule assigning housing by birth sex versus lived identity is documented, no separate units are recorded, and no solitary or segregation practice is documented either. The absence of a documented practice does not establish what happens in a given facility.

The legislative status of both Senate bills after November 2017 is unresolved: the sources record them awaiting a Chamber of Deputies vote and nothing later. Whether either measure has since been enacted, amended or abandoned is not sourced here.

No trans-specific violence rate is available for Haiti in this inventory. There are no counts with denominators, no per-capita comparison against the national homicide rate, and no trend series; the record supplies one identified killing, that of Charlot Jeudy in November 2019, which cannot be ranked against other jurisdictions or read as a prevalence figure.

Entry, visa and document-marker rules are not sourced in this inventory, so what a passport or identity document's sex marker triggers at Haitian border control remains unverified. Nor is any airport-screening treatment specific to trans or gender-nonconforming travellers documented here.

Whether the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs presently operates as written, and how frequently refusal on homosexuality grounds is invoked, is not quantified in these sources.
